proof_attempts.sketch:
Even case: for n=2m, 4/n=2/m=1/m+1/(2m)+1/(2m). Verify: 1/m+1/(2m)+1/(2m)=1/m+1/m=2/m ✓. This is a complete proof for all even n≥2.

Odd n≡3 mod 4: (n+1) is divisible by 4, so let m=(n+1)/4 (positive integer). Then 1/m=4/(n+1). Compute 4/n-1/m=4/n-4/(n+1)=4/(n(n+1)). So 4/n=1/m+4/(n(n+1))=1/((n+1)/4)+4/(n(n+1)). Now 4/(n(n+1))=1/(n(n+1)/4) since 4|(n+1). So 4/n=1/((n+1)/4)+1/(n(n+1)/4). Still only 2 terms. Split first term: 1/((n+1)/4)=1/((n+1)/4+1)+1/(((n+1)/4)((n+1)/4+1))=[COMPLEX]. Alternatively: 4/n=1/n+3/n. For n≡3 mod 4, 3/n=3/n. Take y=(n+1)/4: 1/y=4/(n+1), and 3/n-4/(n+1)=(3n+3-4n)/(n(n+1))=(3-n)/(n(n+1))<0 for n>3. So y must be larger. Try y=n: 3/n-1/n=2/n. Now 2/n with n odd: 2/n=1/((n+1)/2)+1/(n(n+1)/2). So 4/n=1/n+1/((n+1)/2)+1/(n(n+1)/2) for odd n. Verify n=3: 1/3+1/2+1/6=2/6+3/6+1/6=6/6=1=4/... wait 4/3≠1. Error: 1/3+1/2+1/6=2/6+3/6+1/6=1≠4/3. The formula gives 4/n=1/n+2/n=3/n≠4/n. [FLAWED]

Correct attempt for n odd: 4/n=2/n+2/n. Use 2/n=1/((n+1)/2)+1/(n(n+1)/2) (valid for odd n since (n+1)/2 is integer). So 4/n=1/((n+1)/2)+1/(n(n+1)/2)+2/n. But 2/n remains. This is circular.

Correct even case proof stands. Odd case remains open — strategy only.
proof_attempts.checker_feedback: Even-case sub-proof VALID: 1/m+1/(2m)+1/(2m)=2/m=4/(2m) ✓. Odd n≡3 mod 4 sub-proof FLAWED: the identity 4/n=1/n+1/((n+1)/2)+1/(n(n+1)/2) sums to 3/n not 4/n. The 2-term identity 4/n=1/((n+1)/4)+1/(n(n+1)/4) is arithmetically correct but gives only 2 terms. Recommendation: extract even-case as standalone valid proof; use split 1/a=1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1)) on the 2-term identity to get 3 terms for n≡3 mod 4.

proof_attempts.sketch:
COMPLETE PROOFS:

**Even n (n=2m):** 4/n=1/m+1/(2m)+1/(2m)=2/m=4/n. ✓ Complete.

**n≡3 mod 4 (n=4k+3, k≥0):** Let a=(n+1)/4=k+1 (positive integer).
Claim: 4/n=1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1))+1/(na).
Proof: RHS=a/(a(a+1))+1/(a(a+1))+1/(na)=(a+1)/(a(a+1))+1/(na)=1/a+1/(na)=(n+1)/(na)=(n+1)/(n(n+1)/4)=4/n. ✓
All denominators a+1, a(a+1), na are positive integers since a=(n+1)/4∈ℤ₊. COMPLETE.

Verified: n=3(a=1): 1/2+1/2+1/3=4/3 ✓; n=7(a=2): 1/3+1/6+1/14=4/7 ✓; n=11(a=3): 1/4+1/12+1/33=4/11 ✓.

**n≡1 mod 4:** Reduction: with x=(n+3)/4=k+1, we get 4/n=1/(k+1)+12/(n(n+3)). Need 12/(n(n+3))=1/y+1/z. Computationally verified to hold for all n≤200 but no uniform algebraic identity found.
proof_attempts.checker_feedback: Even case: 1/m+1/(2m)+1/(2m)=2/m=4/(2m) ✓. n≡3 mod 4: Step 1: 1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1))=1/a ✓. Step 2: 1/a+1/(na)=(n+1)/(na) ✓. Step 3: (n+1)/(na)=(n+1)/(n(n+1)/4)=4/n ✓. All denominators are positive integers: a+1=(n+5)/4∈ℤ since n≡3 mod 4→4|n+5; a(a+1)=(n+1)(n+5)/16∈ℤ since 4|n+1 and 4|n+5; na=n(n+1)/4∈ℤ since 4|n+1. Verified n=3,7,11. VALID and complete for even n and n≡3 mod 4.

proof_attempts.sketch:
n≡9 mod 12 COMPLETE: n=3j with j≡3 mod 4. Let b=(n+3)/4. Claim: 4/n=1/(b+1)+1/(b(b+1))+1/(jb). Proof: 1/(b+1)+1/(b(b+1))=1/b. Then 1/b+1/(jb)=(j+1)/(jb)=(j+1)/(j(n+3)/4). Now n=3j so (j+1)/(3j(3j+3)/4×(1/j))... let me verify directly: 1/b+1/(jb)=(j+1)/(jb). jb=j(n+3)/4. And 4/n=4/(3j). Need (j+1)/(j(n+3)/4)=4/(3j): (j+1)·4/(j(n+3))=4/(3j) iff 3(j+1)=n+3=3j+3=3(j+1) ✓. COMPLETE.

n≡5 mod 12 COMPLETE (correcting earlier error): n≡5 mod 12 means n≡1 mod 4 AND n≡2 mod 3. Then n+3≡2 mod 3, so 3∤n+3, 3∤b. BUT: 3/(nb) with n≡2 mod 3 and b=(n+3)/4≡? mod 3. n+3≡2 mod 3, so 4b=n+3≡2 mod 3, b≡2·4⁻¹≡2·1≡2 mod 3 (since 4≡1 mod 3). So nb≡2·2=4≡1 mod 3. Need 3/(nb) as 2-term EF with nb≡1 mod 3.
Factorisation: (nb)²=d₁d₂, d₁≡-nb≡2 mod 3. Take d₁=nb-3k for some k... Try d₁=nb+1 (which is ≡2 mod 3 since nb≡1 mod 3): then d₂=(nb)²/(nb+1). For this to be integer, need (nb+1)|(nb)²=(nb+1-1)²=(nb+1)²-2(nb+1)+1, so (nb+1)|1. Fails. Try d₁=(nb-1)/... nb≡1 mod 3, nb-1≡0 mod 3=3t. d₂=(nb)²/(3t)=nb(nb+1)/... hmm need exact divisors.

Alternative for n≡5 mod 12: use anchor x=n. Then 3/n needed as 2-term EF. n≡2 mod 3: write n=3q+2. 3/n=3/(3q+2). Use: 3/(3q+2)=1/(q+1)+1/((q+1)(3q+2)). Check: (3q+2+1)/((q+1)(3q+2))=(3q+3)/((q+1)(3q+2))=3(q+1)/((q+1)(3q+2))=3/(3q+2)=3/n. ✓ So 4/n=1/n+1/(q+1)+1/((q+1)n) where q=(n-2)/3. All positive integers since n≡2 mod 3 → 3|n-2 → q=(n-2)/3∈ℤ₊. COMPLETE FOR n≡5 mod 12.
Verify n=5 (q=1): 1/5+1/2+1/10=2/10+5/10+1/10=8/10=4/5 ✓. n=17 (q=5): 1/17+1/6+1/102=6/102+17/102+1/102=24/102=4/17 ✓. n=29 (q=9): 1/29+1/10+1/290=10/290+29/290+1/290=40/290=4/29 ✓. 

Status: n≡1 mod 4 now split into 3 sub-cases: n≡9 mod 12 ✓, n≡5 mod 12 ✓, n≡1 mod 12 (OPEN). The n≡1 mod 12 case is the last open case of the entire conjecture.
